prompt: Write an essay on why building subways costs so much more in some countries than in others. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
A kilometer of new subway in New York has cost well over a billion dollars; the Second Avenue Subway's first phase came in at roughly $2.5 billion per kilometer. In Madrid, Seoul, Stockholm, or Milan, comparable tunnels have been built for a tenth of that, sometimes less. The gap cannot be explained by wages, since Sweden and Italy are not low-wage countries, nor by geology, density, or archaeology, since Rome and Istanbul dig through millennia of buried history at a fraction of American prices. The difference lies mostly in how projects are designed, managed, and governed.

The largest single driver is what gets built. Stations, not tunnels, dominate the cost of modern subways, and expensive countries build enormous ones. Researchers at NYU's Transit Costs Project found that the Second Avenue Subway's stations were far larger than the trains required, with full-length mezzanines and extensive back-of-house space, because each operating department demanded its own rooms rather than sharing facilities. Stations were mined deep underground to avoid disrupting the street, a method several times more expensive than cutting a trench and covering it. Low-cost cities accept some months of surface disruption, standardize station designs so that each one is not a bespoke architectural project, and size them for the trains they serve. Madrid's great expansion of the 1990s and 2000s used a handful of repeated station templates and simple, shallow construction wherever possible.

The second driver is who manages the work. Agencies in Spain, Italy, South Korea, and France maintain permanent in-house staffs of engineers who plan projects, supervise contractors, and make technical decisions quickly. In the United States, Britain, and other English-speaking countries, public agencies hollowed out this capacity over decades and now rely on consultants for design, project management, and even the oversight of other consultants. This is costly in direct fees, but the larger damage is indirect. An agency without expertise cannot evaluate a contractor's claims, cannot resolve field problems promptly, and cannot tell a reasonable change order from an opportunistic one. Decisions drift upward and stall. Contractors, knowing the client is slow and adversarial, price that risk into their bids. In New York, soft costs for design and management have added far more to construction budgets than they do in continental Europe.

Procurement compounds the problem. Low-cost countries tend to break projects into moderate-sized contracts, award them on technical merit as well as price, and pay for itemized quantities so that changes can be priced without litigation. High-cost countries have often favored huge design-build contracts that transfer as much risk as possible to the private sector. The theory is that risk transfer disciplines contractors; in practice, firms charge heavily for risks they cannot control, few are large enough to bid, and competition thins. When disputes arise, they are settled by lawyers rather than engineers.

Labor matters too, though less through wages than through staffing. Investigations of New York's projects found tunnel boring machines operated by crews several times larger than those used in Europe, along with positions preserved by work rules long after technology made them unnecessary. Yet labor is easy to overemphasize. Heavily unionized, well-paid Scandinavian workers build cheaply, because their projects use fewer workers more productively. The trouble arises where agencies have no seat at the bargaining table, as when contractors negotiate with unions and pass the bill to the public.

Behind all of this sits politics. Infrastructure in the high-cost world is built under conditions that give many parties a veto and few the authority to decide. Environmental review can take years and invites litigation, so agencies design defensively, buying off opposition with expensive mitigations. Utilities, neighboring governments, and other agencies extract concessions, such as a rebuilt street or a new park, as the price of cooperation. Funding arrives irregularly, so each line is treated as a once-in-a-generation event, loaded with every stakeholder's wishes, rather than as one step in a continuous program. Countries that build continuously keep experienced teams and supply chains intact; those that build one line every thirty years relearn the craft each time.

One further pattern stands out: the costliest systems are concentrated in the English-speaking world, and costs have risen in places that imported its practices. Canada, Singapore, and Hong Kong built affordably a generation ago and now do not. This suggests that the problem is contagious, spread by a shared consulting industry and a shared ideology of privatized expertise, and also that it is curable, since nothing about it is fixed by nature.

The lesson from cheap builders is unglamorous. Hire and retain public engineers, and trust them to decide. Standardize designs, dig shallow, and tolerate temporary disruption. Keep contracts small and flexible. Build steadily rather than episodically. None of this requires new technology. It requires governments to treat construction as a core competence rather than something to be purchased, and the cities that have done so are still expanding their networks while others debate whether they can afford a single extension.
